newsitem.title: USA: Northeast states ask EPA to cut smog from Midwest.
newsitem.headline: Northeast states ask EPA to cut smog from Midwest.

text.p: Eight northeastern states asked the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Thursday to force power plants and factories from Alabama to Wisconsin to cut their pollution to help get rid of smog downwind.

Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island and Vermont pressed for new curbs on big emitters of smog-forming nitrogen oxides in the eastern half of the country, which they said were blowing smog into their region.

"Many power plants outside the Northeast do little or nothing to control their emissions, creating a health hazard in downwind states," said Vermont's Attorney General William Sorrell. "It is only right that these sources of our air pollution ... do their share to clean up the air."

Northeastern states have long struggled to meet federal clean air standards and last June signed onto an agreement reached by 32 eastern states to take steps to help each other combat smog in cities with the dirtiest air.

Using the June agreement, the EPA plans to tell each of the states next month how much pollution they will have to trim to meet federal ozone limits in their own states and to help other states meet the standard.

One of the agreement's key recommendations was a call for power plants to cut their nitrogen oxides emissions by 50 percent to 85 percent. The states' petitions Thursday were designed to make sure the EPA enforces those limits and to speed up action to cut pollution.

"This summer Pennsylvania has exceeded the ozone standard 21 times," Pennsylvania's Environmental Protection Secretary James Seif said, adding that one-third of Pennsylvania's pollution came from other states.
"EPA needs to act quickly to address the issue of transport of air pollution for us to avoid those violations in the summers to come," he said in a statement.

Under the Clean Air Act, the EPA has 60 days to act on the petitions and decide whether to require specific plants to cut their emissions within three years to help stop the drift. If the problem is serious enough, the EPA can force the targeted plants to shut down within three months.
But EPA Assistant Administrator Mary Nichols said the agency had never ordered any facilities to stop production and had no plans to do so now.

"We're not going to be shutting any plants down," Nichols said in an interview. "Everyone's goal is to get maximum cleanup from these major sources ... that have not done their share of the cleanup compared to other industries in America."
Nichols said it would be unrealistic to expect big factories and power generators to be able to install new equipment to clean their smokestacks in less than five years.
She downplayed the urgency of the petitions, saying they fit with the agency's plan to set regional caps on nitrogen oxides emissions and to allow trading of emissions credits by under the cap.
